tagline.text: A student-town food and cafe strip in Quezon City

location.label: Location
location.text: Maginhawa Street, UP Village and Teachers Village area, Quezon City

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (festival on the first Saturday of December)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half a day to a full day

children.text: Maginhawa Street is a food street in Quezon City next to the University of the Philippines Diliman campus, where restaurants, cafes and food parks line a stretch of about
2.2km
. The city has designated it a tourism district, and it is busy with cafes by day and late-night food and bars after dark.

Maginhawa Street runs through UP Village and Teachers Village in Quezon City, Metro Manila. Close to the University of the Philippines Diliman campus, it attracts students and young professionals, and since around 2010 small eateries have gradually multiplied until the street became known as a food destination. In Tagalog, the name means "comfortable" or "relaxed." It borders the south side of the UP Diliman campus, so lunch crowds are mostly students, while evenings bring office workers and families.

In 2015, Quezon City designated the area as a tourism district called the Maginhawa Art and Food Hub under Ordinance No. 2439 (S-2015), and in 2017 Ordinance No. 2559 (S-2017) extended it to Mayaman Street. The district is about
2.2km
long and, besides the main Maginhawa road, includes the side-street eateries of V. Luna Extension, Malingap, Magiting and Mayaman.
Prices range from a pizza at around
to main dishes at around

, which makes it feel like a neighborhood food street rather than the upscale dining districts of Makati or BGC. A tapsilog diner said to date back to 1949, a garden cafe, an Italian trattoria, an ice cream shop, a food-truck park, a Japanese ramen shop and a hidden cocktail bar all sit on one street, so it suits a "food crawl" where you walk and sample many places.
There have also been recent attempts to reshape the street around people. From November 2024 to February 2025, the city and civic groups ran a "tactical urbanism" trial on a

stretch, turning one lane into a shared path for pedestrians and cyclists and another into a public gathering space, with temporary one-way traffic. The trial period has ended, so check the current road layout on site. It is not a polished tourist attraction: shops change often, and parking and traffic are difficult. Shop details here are based on guides from around 2025, so check current hours and menus before you go.
Rodic's Diner at 129 Maginhawa is a no-frills eatery famous for tapsilog (a plate of beef tapa with garlic rice and egg). It is described as serving this plate since 1949, and it opens at
, which makes it a good breakfast stop. Hours vary by day, so confirm before a late visit.
This garden-style cafe and restaurant at No. 44 is known for dishes such as crispy pork belly adobo (about
) and lengua pasta (about
). It gets crowded on weekends, so it is safer to book ahead.
Food parks such as StrEAT at No. 91 Maginhawa gather several food trucks and pop-up restaurants, which works well for groups with different tastes. The lineup changes often.

Pino Restaurant (Filipino dishes), Escapee speakeasy and Flying House on Malingap Street are all a few minutes' walk from one another. Pino is known for Filipino dishes such as kare-kareng bagnet (about
Cafes such as SGD Coffee Bodega (on Maalalahanin Street) and X Wave Specialty Coffee (2nd floor, No. 80) line the street. As in any college town, many people settle in with a laptop for hours.

Foreign restaurants such as Mugen Ramenya, Crazy Katsu, Friuli Trattoria and Namnam20 are on the same street, giving you plenty of options when you tire of Filipino food. Mugen Ramenya does not take reservations, so expect to queue.
This ice cream shop at the corner of Maginhawa and Mapagkumbaba streets is a good place to finish a walk with dessert at the southern end. It is about
1km
from Talisay.

Under the ordinance that created the tourism district, the Maginhawa Arts and Food Festival is said to be held every first Saturday of December. Details and road closures change from year to year, so check the latest announcements.

items.title: Half-day food crawl
items.subtitle: From tapsilog for breakfast to late-night eats

children.text: Start with tapsilog for breakfast at Rodic's Diner. It is less crowded if you go early.
Walk along the main Maginhawa road and have coffee at a cafe (SGD Coffee Bodega, X Wave and others) while taking in the street scene.
Take a long lunch at Talisay The Garden Cafe or Pino Restaurant. On weekends, call ahead to check for a table.
Pick up snacks at a food park, then finish with ice cream at Papa Diddi's.
For dinner, arrive when the doors open at places with long lines, including Mugen Ramenya, and wait in the queue.
At about
2.2km
, Maginhawa can be walked end to end at a leisurely pace, but the middle of the street clogs up at night. It is easier to walk it one section at a time.
Have an early dinner at Pino Restaurant on Malingap Street.
Have a drink at a nearby bar (Mugen, Escapee speakeasy and others). Escapee is described as a hidden bar behind a bookshelf inside a Japanese fried chicken shop.
To head home, book a Grab ahead of time and get in at a main road.

Friday and Saturday nights are the busiest. For a calmer visit, choose a weekday evening. Bars that stay open late have different hours each day, so confirm before you go and arrange your ride home in advance.
Take a Grab or taxi from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) to Quezon City. Depending on the time of day, it can take
1–2 hours
During rush hours (weekdays
and
), the trip takes much longer, so allow extra time.
Fares vary widely by time of day, so check the fare in the app on arrival.
From Makati, BGC, Malate and similar areas, Grab is the easiest option. Set your drop-off at the address of the shop where you plan to start on Maginhawa Street.
Maginhawa Street is about
2.2km
long, so once you pick a starting point you can walk the rest.
Within Quezon City, a short Grab ride from UP Diliman or nearby malls is a common way to get there. Check fares locally.
Jeepneys and tricycles run around Quezon City, but routes change, so check locally.
On the street itself you mostly walk, and heading toward the university campus brings you to UP Diliman.
Maginhawa is cafe-centered by day and restaurant-and-bar-centered at night. Weekday afternoons are the quietest, and Friday and Saturday nights are the busiest.
In the rainy season, streets can flood and traffic can slow, so the dry season is the safer choice.
Popular restaurants have waits even on weekend afternoons. Avoiding mealtimes (
and
) can shorten your wait, and at the end of the year expect road closures and crowds because of the festival on the first Saturday of December, so check the latest announcements.

Maginhawa Street itself has few hotels, so most visitors stay elsewhere in Quezon City or in Makati or BGC and come for the day. If you do stay in Quezon City, somewhere near UP Diliman is convenient. Check rates and availability for lodging yourself. If Maginhawa is the whole point of your trip, it is more efficient to plan a day visit than to book a separate stay.

The food ranges from traditional Filipino dishes to Japanese, Italian and Vietnamese. For a quick bite, pick a food park; for a sit-down meal, choose a restaurant on the Malingap lane. Shops change often, so check recent Google Maps reviews and opening hours.

For a rough order of the day: a hearty plate such as tapsilog or a Filipino breakfast set in the morning, a garden cafe restaurant for lunch, cafes and ice cream in the afternoon, ramen or a restaurant like Pino for dinner, and the bars on Malingap at night. With a big group, ordering different dishes at a food park and sharing is easy. If you need a vegetarian or halal diet, menus differ from shop to shop, so ask directly.
Weekday afternoons are quiet, while Friday and Saturday nights bring long lines. For popular places, go when the doors open.
Most places are walk-in, but for groups at places like Talisay or Pino, call ahead.
Mugen Ramenya takes no reservations, and the wait can exceed
1 hour
Small shops may mostly take cash or GCash, so carry some small bills.
Grab pickups are quicker if you set the pickup point on a main road.
Pino, SGD, Escapee and Flying House are a few minutes' walk from one another, so they are easy to combine.
Papa Diddi's is about
1km
south of Talisay, which makes it a good end to a walk.
If you plan to stay long at a cafe, check the outlets and Wi-Fi first. In a college town, seats fill up fast.
Bring an umbrella and wet wipes. Many alley restaurants have outdoor seating, so rain and heat affect you.
In the evening the middle of Maginhawa is badly congested with parked and moving cars, and overnight street parking may be restricted.
Overnight and long-term street parking on the street is restricted, so use a paid basement car park.
Business hours and menus change often. Check the latest information before you visit.
In the rainy season, flooding and traffic delays are possible, so leave room in your schedule.
At night, keep your belongings in front of you and avoid staring at your phone in the street for long.
Because of the road project (including the 2024–2025 trial section), parts of the street have been one-way, so check your drop-off point in advance.
Ratings differ widely between review sites. Do not rely on a single review; compare several places.
A city park you can reach by car from Maginhawa (travel time depends on traffic), good for walking and exercise.
A mixed-use district east of Quezon City where you can enjoy shopping, restaurants and a lively night atmosphere.
A university campus next to Maginhawa with wide grounds and walking paths. Check entry rules locally. You can also pair a meal on Maginhawa with a walk around the campus.
